description: Working on the project regarding health monitoring software - I’m Sophia, I have an interest in biochem, physics and astronomy; join if you’re similar!
summary:
CHIRON

Space exploration has already shown that medical emergencies can arise in unexpected ways, even among highly trained astronauts. During Apollo 13, astronaut Fred Haise developed a urinary tract infection while travelling back to Earth, with limited suitable medication available onboard. Decades later, an astronaut aboard the International Space Station was found to have a blood clot in the internal jugular vein, highlighting how unexpected medical conditions can arise in space and how challenging they can be to assess and manage.

CHIRON aims to address these challenges by bringing together the knowledge, tools and coordination needed to support astronaut health throughout a mission. It combines personalised health monitoring, medical preparation, emergency coordination and ongoing wellbeing support within one connected platform. Through its proposed LINK devices, including smartwatches, augmented-reality glasses and spacesuit displays, this support could also extend beyond the central workstation, making essential information and medical guidance more accessible wherever astronauts are working.

Inspired by Chiron, the Greek mythological healer and teacher, our project is built on a simple belief: as humanity explores farther, the ability to care for one another must travel with us.
details:
CHIRON: The Health System Astronauts Truly Need

The farther humanity explores, the more important it becomes to ensure that the people undertaking these journeys have access to reliable medical support. Space exploration places the human body in an environment it was never designed for, creating challenges that require continuous monitoring, preparation and care. Astronauts need more than a system that responds when something goes wrong; they need one that helps them understand their health, maintain their medical knowledge and manage potential medical situations throughout their missions.

CHIRON is our answer to this need: an integrated medical support system that brings together prevention, preparation, emergency response, recovery and continuity. Rather than functioning as just another emergency application, it aims to support astronauts throughout their entire journey, helping them care for themselves and one another while making medical knowledge and resources more accessible.

The idea behind CHIRON

CHIRON takes its name from the healer and teacher of Greek mythology, who trained Asclepius in the art of medicine. This idea of combining knowledge, guidance and care forms the foundation of our project.

We wanted to create a system that does more than tell astronauts what to do. It should also help them understand their own health, maintain their medical knowledge and feel prepared to care for themselves and their crew mates. Medical training received before launch may become difficult to recall months or years into a mission, particularly when an unfamiliar situation arises. CHIRON therefore incorporates short educational refreshers and practical rehearsals that help astronauts retain and apply what they have learned.

How the system works

At the centre of CHIRON is CORE, the main system that brings together information from wearable devices, medical equipment, astronaut check-ins, the spacecraft and Earth. It uses this information to support five interconnected stages of medical care: prevention, training and preparation, emergency response, recovery and continuity.

These stages are supported by several shared components: a Medical Library containing approved medical guidance, a Medical Inventory tracking available supplies, Mission Context adapting the system to the environment, a Response Planner coordinating medical situations, and an individual CHIRON ID connecting information to each astronaut's medical profile.

The system is designed to adapt to different exploration environments. Our prototype includes four simulated missions: the International Space Station, a lunar mission, transit to Mars and the Martian surface. Each has its own communication delay, gravity conditions, radiation exposure and available medical supplies. This allows the same system to behave differently depending on where the crew is and what resources they can access.

Prevention: understanding health before problems arise

CHIRON begins by helping astronauts monitor their health on a daily basis. It focuses on six indicators relevant to the challenge: heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep and mood.

Information can come directly from connected devices, such as a wearable heart-rate monitor, chest strap, blood pressure cuff, glucose meter or thermometer. Alternatively, astronauts can enter their readings manually or report them through voice input. A daily check-in brings these measurements together in one place.

Rather than relying on universal thresholds alone, CHIRON compares readings with each astronaut's individual baseline, taking their medical history into account. This information can be entered and reviewed by the flight surgeon before launch. Mission conditions also influence what the system monitors more closely. For example, as the crew approaches Mars, CHIRON can place greater emphasis on muscle condition, balance and blood pressure in preparation for changes in gravity.

Importantly, the system does not assume that normal sensor readings mean an astronaut is healthy. Crew members can report symptoms independently, and CHIRON's symptom checker considers these reports alongside available measurements and medical history to suggest possible explanations and appropriate next steps.

Mental health is treated as an equally important part of astronaut wellbeing. Mood check-ins remain private, while CHIRON can identify patterns involving mood, sleep and reaction time that may warrant attention. A dedicated distress-support feature first considers possible physical causes and then offers breathing exercises, grounding techniques or a confidential request for assistance from a chosen crew mate or flight psychologist.

To avoid giving misleading information, CHIRON distinguishes between the source of a reading, whether the value passes technical validity checks, and whether it has been clinically reviewed. Missing measurements remain clearly identified as missing, while outdated information is labelled as the last known reading rather than being presented as current.

Training and preparation: keeping medical knowledge accessible

Medical training cannot end when astronauts leave Earth. Procedures learned months before launch may need to be recalled under pressure, in an unfamiliar environment and without immediate guidance from medical professionals.

CHIRON addresses this through its Medical Library and training system. The library contains guides for medical devices and procedures, explaining how equipment should be used, what its readings mean and when medical review is necessary. Its contents are designed to remain accessible throughout a mission.

The training component tracks each astronaut's practice history and identifies procedures that may need refreshing. It also allows the crew to rehearse the same emergency workflows they would encounter in a real situation.

Before a mission or an emergency, the preparation feature evaluates the crew's readiness using the available personnel, equipment, protocols and communication delays. It identifies gaps and turns them into practical recommendations. For example, if an astronaut has not practised a particular procedure for several months, CHIRON can suggest that they complete a refresher.

Training and readiness are kept separate from medical authorisation: completing a training exercise does not automatically qualify someone to perform every medical procedure.

Emergency response: coordinating care when it matters most

In an emergency, CHIRON can be activated from any screen through a dedicated emergency button or voice command. All connected devices then switch to a shared emergency interface, allowing the crew to follow the same situation as it develops.

The central component is the Response Planner. Instead of presenting isolated medical information, it brings together the patient's symptoms, readings and medical history with the mission environment, available equipment, crew members' training, their proximity to the patient and the time required to communicate with Earth.

Using this information, CHIRON matches the situation to an approved medical procedure and explains why that procedure is relevant, what information supports it and what resources may be missing. It presents practical steps, identifies alternatives where appropriate and updates follow-up tasks as new information becomes available.

The system does not diagnose medical conditions, prescribe medication or invent treatments and dosages. It relies on approved procedures and published first-aid guidance, with medication use limited to the patient's prescribed medical supplies and their existing instructions.

CHIRON also helps coordinate the people involved. Tasks are proposed only to suitable crew members who are available, appropriately trained and not the patient. Suggestions are ranked according to factors such as proximity, training recency and workload. However, no assignment becomes active until the designated response lead confirms it. If circumstances change, the assignment returns to a proposed state for review.

Everyone receives the necessary emergency notification, but only those needed for a particular task are assigned responsibilities. At any point, the crew can access an explanation of how CHIRON reached its recommendations, including the information used, the rules applied and the limitations of its decision.

Because communication with Earth may be delayed, CHIRON also prepares medical reports automatically. Each report has a visible status, showing whether it has been prepared, queued, transmitted, received, reviewed or answered. This means astronauts can continue following their onboard procedures without assuming that Earth has already received or responded to their information.

The Medical Inventory works alongside the Response Planner, tracking quantities, locations, expiry dates and equipment maintenance. Supplies reserved for an ongoing emergency are accounted for, and only approved alternatives are suggested when something is unavailable.

Recovery and continuity: caring beyond the emergency

Medical support does not end when an emergency is over. Astronauts may need to follow recovery plans, monitor their progress and receive continued medical attention throughout the remainder of their mission.

CHIRON's recovery component turns flight-surgeon-authorised recovery plans into daily checklists, allowing astronauts to follow their progress against their normal health measurements. Missing information is never interpreted as evidence of recovery.

The continuity component ensures that medical information remains accessible even when devices disconnect or crew responsibilities change. Every reading, decision and action is recorded in a chronological medical timeline, allowing another crew member or medical officer to understand what has happened and take over when necessary.

An additional feature is the Medical State Capsule: an offline copy of an astronaut's essential medical information stored on their wearable device. This allows important records to remain accessible even without a network connection. When the device reconnects, its locally recorded information is synchronised with the central system. If the same record has been changed in both locations, the conflict is referred to a medical officer rather than silently overwriting either version.

Privacy and individual medical profiles

Medical information is particularly sensitive, especially in the close living environment of a spacecraft. CHIRON therefore separates general crew status from individual medical records.

The shared dashboard displays only general health statuses, while each astronaut's personal profile is protected by an individual PIN. (For demonstration purposes, each astronaut profile also includes a "Press for demo password" option beneath the keypad, allowing users to access the profile using its demonstration password.) Medical officers can access profiles using their own credentials, and emergency access is available when necessary, provided a reason is recorded. These access events are logged and can be reviewed by the profile owner.

During an emergency, devices can switch to the shared emergency interface so that the crew can coordinate care without leaving important information inaccessible.

Research foundation

CHIRON's design is informed by existing NASA research and guidance on human health during space exploration. Rather than starting entirely from scratch, we used NASA's existing research and medical data as a foundation, building upon the information already available and identifying what additional elements would be needed to support our proposed system.

NASA-STD-3001, Volume 1, informed our approach to crew health, medical responsibilities and confidential communication. Volume 2 influenced the interface design, particularly the use of large, accessible controls and clear alerts suitable for demanding spacecraft environments.

NASA's research into Earth-independent medical operations helped shape our approach to offline functionality and the Medical State Capsule. The Human Research Roadmap and identified medical capability gaps, including Medical-401 and Medical-701, informed our monitoring, resource management and emergency planning features.

We also incorporated information from NASA's Open Science Data Repository, using its existing research records as a foundation for CHIRON's research and data components. We built upon the available information by considering what additional data, organisation and functionality would be required for our system, including astronaut-specific medical profiles, individual health baselines, mission-related information and medical resource tracking. This allowed us to extend the original research foundation into a more comprehensive structure suited to CHIRON's intended purpose. These research records are presented as supporting evidence and are never mistaken for live astronaut measurements.

CHIRON builds upon these existing concepts and research. It is an independent project and is not endorsed by NASA.

Artificial intelligence and transparency

An important design decision was to avoid relying on AI to make medical decisions. CHIRON's Response Planner, symptom checker, readiness assessments, crew-task ranking and medical guidance use deterministic rules. This means that the same inputs produce the same results, making recommendations easier to trace, explain and verify.

The current prototype uses the browser's built-in speech recognition to convert spoken input into text. This is the only machine-learning component currently used. A real mission implementation would require speech recognition capable of operating independently of an internet connection.

AI is proposed for selected future hardware capabilities, particularly recognising medical equipment and understanding the surrounding environment for augmented-reality guidance. It would not replace the rule-based medical decision-making system.

What we have built: the working prototype

CHIRON is currently implemented as a working web application. Our prototype focuses on demonstrating how the different components interact rather than claiming to provide a clinically validated medical system.

Implemented features include the shared crew dashboard, PIN-protected astronaut profiles, daily health check-ins, a body map, symptom checker, Medical Library, baseline approval, emergency mode, Response Planner, confirmed task assignments, Earth medical reports, alert tracking, readiness assessments, recovery tracking, the medical event log and the Medical State Capsule.

The Medical Library also supports integrity-checked content updates through a Mission Control console.

To demonstrate how CHIRON would behave in space, the prototype uses simulated crew members, medical records, equipment, inventory, sensor readings, mission scenarios and responses from Earth. Data can synchronise between browser tabs and, through an optional relay, between devices on the same network.

We distinguish between software verification and clinical or operational validation in our testing plan. The current prototype can be tested for software functionality and consistency, but its medical workflows have not yet been validated for real astronaut use.

How we developed it

We began by researching NASA's work on exploration medicine and identifying the medical needs our project should address. We then translated these requirements into individual features and developed the application through short building and testing cycles, evaluating each scenario from the perspective of an astronaut using the system.

Our team collaborated through GitHub, working on separate branches before merging the features into a shared application.

The software was developed using TypeScript, React 18 and Vite, with Tailwind CSS for styling and three.js for the interactive three-dimensional space background. Node.js scripts support device synchronisation through WebSockets and the retrieval of research data from NASA's repository. We also used browser capabilities such as speech recognition, cross-tab communication and local storage.

Claude Code and GitHub Copilot assisted with writing and reviewing code under our direction. The team remained responsible for the system architecture, feature design, medical logic, research decisions and final implementation.

Link containing code: https://github.com/arithmetica-m/Nasa-Space-apps

Our team and collaboration

CHIRON was developed collaboratively by our three team members: Sophia, Maria and Celina. Throughout the project, we worked together to brainstorm ideas, explore different approaches and identify ways to make the system more useful, practical and innovative. Rather than settling on our initial concepts, we continuously revisited our decisions, discussed potential improvements and refined individual features as the project developed.

Each stage involved exchanging feedback, identifying weaknesses and finding ways to improve both the functionality and the overall experience of using CHIRON. Through repeated discussions, revisions and testing, we gradually developed our original idea into a more comprehensive and connected system. Our final project is the result of this ongoing collaboration, with each team member contributing to the development and refinement of the overall concept.

Future development: custom astronaut profiles and database expansion

Another planned improvement is to allow users to add new astronauts and their medical information directly to CHIRON. Instead of relying exclusively on the simulated crew members already included in the prototype, the system could support the creation of individual astronaut profiles using a standardised data format.

Users would be able to prepare an astronaut's information in a predefined template containing the necessary identifiers, medical history, baseline measurements and other relevant health information. Once completed and checked against the required format, the file could be uploaded and integrated into CHIRON's database, automatically creating a corresponding profile.

This would make the system more adaptable to different crews and missions, allowing medical information to be prepared before launch and updated as necessary. It would also make CHIRON easier to demonstrate and test with different simulated astronauts, medical histories and health conditions, without requiring changes to the underlying application.

In a real implementation, this process would include appropriate authentication, validation and medical approval to ensure that information is accurate, secure and associated with the correct astronaut.

Future extensions: CHIRON LINK hardware

Although the current project is a software prototype, we envision CHIRON eventually extending into a connected hardware ecosystem known as CHIRON LINK. Rather than developing three independent devices, the idea is to create complementary interfaces that connect to CORE through the spacecraft's onboard network and are associated with each astronaut's CHIRON ID.

The first proposed device is the LINK Watch, a wrist-worn wearable that collects health readings, supports daily check-ins and displays alerts. With onboard positioning beacons, it could also help identify the approximate location of crew members, allowing the Response Planner to consider who is closest to an emergency. Position information would include its timestamp and accuracy, with outdated readings clearly identified as uncertain.

The second is LINK Vision, a pair of AI-enabled augmented-reality glasses. These would recognise medical equipment, help astronauts locate supplies and display approved procedural guidance within their field of view. For example, an astronaut could receive visual guidance on finding and using a particular medical device without repeatedly looking away from the situation. If the glasses lose environmental tracking, they would clearly indicate that guidance is unavailable rather than displaying potentially misplaced instructions.

Finally, LINK Helmet would extend CHIRON to compatible spacesuit visors during extravehicular activities. It would provide large, high-contrast controls, persistent critical alerts and voice interaction through the suit microphone, designed to remain usable while wearing gloves. It would complement existing spacesuit safety systems, never replace them.

All three devices would communicate their own limitations, including low battery, failed connections, unavailable sensors and lost positioning or environmental tracking.

Other proposed extensions include fingerprint-based identification alongside PIN and badge alternatives, digitally signed Medical Library updates, a defined policy for permissions when operating offline and risk models validated by medical teams. Offline permissions would account for the possibility that access changes made on Earth cannot take effect until a connection is restored.

Voice-activated assistant

CHIRON could incorporate an advanced voice-activated assistant inspired by the functionality of JARVIS in Marvel. Rather than requiring astronauts to manually open the application or activate voice controls, the system could remain in a low-power listening mode, waiting for a specific activation phrase such as "Hey, CHIRON" or "CHIRON, can you help me?". Once the phrase is recognised, astronauts could interact with the system through natural speech, requesting medical information, accessing their personal profiles, checking mission-related information or receiving assistance with different tasks. This could be particularly valuable during emergencies, when an astronaut may not have the time or ability to navigate the interface manually. For example, an astronaut could verbally announce an emergency and describe their symptoms, allowing CHIRON to initiate the relevant emergency support procedures. The system could also be designed to operate through compatible headsets, smartwatches or future augmented-reality glasses, making voice interaction accessible without requiring astronauts to be directly in front of a screen.

These developments represent the next stage of CHIRON rather than features already implemented in our current prototype.

Personal wellbeing and quality of life

CHIRON could also include an optional personal space where astronauts can record important milestones, save memorable moments, photographs and personal reflections from their mission. This would allow them to preserve meaningful experiences and maintain a personal connection to their lives beyond the spacecraft. Alongside this, the system could offer a recreation and relaxation section containing activities such as puzzles, creative writing, guided relaxation exercises and other forms of entertainment. Each astronaut would also have a private area for personal notes, preferences and reflections, separate from their medical records and accessible only according to their chosen privacy settings. Although these features would not directly monitor physical health, they could contribute to astronauts' overall wellbeing by encouraging relaxation, self-expression and positive experiences. During long-duration missions, opportunities to take breaks, reflect on personal achievements and maintain a sense of individuality could help reduce feelings of isolation and support psychological health.

Potential applications beyond space exploration

Although CHIRON was designed primarily for astronauts, its underlying concept could also be adapted to support healthcare in remote and underserved communities on Earth. In rural areas where access to medical professionals, reliable internet connections or nearby healthcare facilities may be limited, a similar system could help individuals monitor their health, access medical guidance and maintain essential medical records. Its offline capabilities, organised medical information and ability to support local healthcare workers could make it particularly useful in environments with limited infrastructure. With appropriate adaptations and clinical oversight, CHIRON's technology could therefore extend beyond space exploration, demonstrating how solutions developed for some of the most challenging environments could also contribute to improving healthcare access on Earth.

Our vision

Ultimately, CHIRON is built around a simple idea: astronauts should not lose access to meaningful medical support simply because Earth is far away.

By connecting everyday health monitoring, continuous medical education, coordinated emergency response and long-term recovery, we aim to create a system that allows astronauts to care for themselves and one another throughout the challenges of space exploration.

Because wherever humanity goes, the ability to care for one another should go too.
